summary: Technical deep dive on KV cache eviction/paging behavior observed by Zenon in production. Discussed eviction patterns with long-context sessions, prefix-reuse causing apparent collisions, paging thresholds, and suggested mitigations (shard tuning, prefix normalization, TTLs, dynamic eviction policy). Agreed to run benchmarks with Zenon's traces and iterate on config; follow-up scheduled.
transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2027-11-17
Start: 14:30 UTC
Duration: ~60m
Attendees: Maya (Redwood AE), Ravi (Redwood SE), Lena (Redwood Solutions), Alex (Zenon ML Eng), Priya (Zenon SRE), Tom (Zenon CTO)

[00:00] Maya: Hey everyone thanks for joining, quick round of intros, and then Ravi will jump in on the KV cache findings.
[00:12] Alex: Hey, Alex from Zenon, we handle the ML infra side. Priya and Tom are on for ops and arch questions.
[00:18] Priya: Yep, thanks. We've been seeing higher eviction rates during long user sessions.
[00:25] Ravi: Cool. Quick preview: we'll go over how our runtime shards KV, the paging model, and then walk through your traces. Please interrupt if anything sounds off or if my terms are fuzzy, sometimes the transcription uses odd words.

[00:40] Ravi: Fundamental piece: our KV cache is sharded by key namespace and model shard, each shard has a max_kv_pages value which controls how many 4MB pages we allow before we start evicting. Once a shard hits that budget we run an eviction policy (LRU like with some heuristics).
[01:05] Priya: We're seeing eviction spikes even though overall memory isn't saturated across the node. It looks per-shard. Could that be due to prefix reuse?
[01:15] Ravi: Yes, that's the usual symptom. If multiple different prefixes hash to the same shard or you have many unique prefixes, one shard can get hot and hit its page limit even though other shards are underutilized.
[01:28] Alex: When you say prefix, we're using conversation IDs plus prompt templates. We sometimes inject dynamic user metadata into the prompt, could that cause high cardinality?
[01:37] Ravi: Absolutely. If you have per-user tokens in the prefix, that multiplies distinct KV entries. Prefix reuse can help — reusing canonicalized prefixes — but it needs normalization.

[01:50] Maya: Quick note: we often see teams accidentally include request-scoped IDs in prompts, which explodes the keyspace. Normalizing reduces unique keys and therefore reduces per-shard pressure.

[02:01] Priya: Can you explain paging behaviour? We saw 'paging' in the logs; what's a page here?
[02:08] Ravi: In our implementation a page ~4MB of KV store memory; max_kv_pages is the per-shard budget. When a shard exceeds budget it starts moving older entries to an on-disk page or evicting depending on config. We call it paging when entries are moved out of hot GPU memory — that increases latency on cache miss because we need to fetch and rehydrate.
[02:33] Alex: We're seeing latency jumps when certain sessions go beyond ~10k tokens. Is that consistent with page churn?
[02:39] Ravi: Yes, long-context sessions create lots of KV entries; if they don't reuse prefixes those entries are unique and can push the shard over budget leading to paging or eviction. Paging causes a latency tail because rehydrate can be tens to hundreds of ms depending on whether it's local SSD or networked storage.

[03:00] Tom: We're on a Dedicated pool, right? Do dedicated nodes have different defaults?
[03:06] Maya: Dedicated has same runtime but you can set higher max_kv_pages per shard and bump memory budgets. Also you can pin models to nodes to improve prefix locality.

[03:20] Ravi: A few mitigations we discussed: prefix normalization: canonicalize prompts to remove per-request metadata; shard tuning: increase max_kv_pages for hot shards, or change shard count to rebalance key distribution; eviction policy: switch from strict LRU to age-weighted policy for long-context workloads; session pinning: route long sessions to specific nodes so their KV grows in a controlled way.

[03:55] Priya: About shard count, if we increase shard count won't that increase overhead?
[04:00] Ravi: It can increase metadata overhead but helps spread keys. There's a tradeoff: more shards reduce per-shard pressure but increases global management. For Zenon's profile we recommended slight increase (e.g., 16->24) in preliminary sims.

[04:18] Alex: You mentioned collisions due to hashing; how probable are collisions?
[04:22] Ravi: Hash collisions to the same shard are expected at scale — not collisions in key equality sense — it's about mapping many unique keys to limited shard buckets. The solution is either more shards or better prefix canonicalization to reduce unique keys.

[04:35] Maya: Also note prefix reuse across sessions is a pattern — if two sessions share a prefix we get cache hits and that's great, but if prefixes differ slightly (extra whitespace, different user tag) we lose reuse. We suggest a small client-side normalization library.

[04:55] Priya: About eviction metrics — we saw an eviction_rate of 12% during peak traffic. What's acceptable?
[05:02] Ravi: For long-context workload we'd like to see <5% eviction_rate on hot shards. Above that you'll see throughput/latency regressions. The goal is minimize cold rehydrates into GPU memory.

[05:15] Alex: Is there a way to prioritize which keys to keep? For example we have a small set of high-value system prompts.
[05:22] Ravi: Yes, we support pinning key prefixes or assigning higher retention weight to certain namespaces so they survive eviction longer — effectively a TTL or priority tier. That helps keep golden prefixes in memory.

[05:35] Tom: Does quantization affect KV memory usage? We saw notes in docs about quantization and memory footprint.
[05:42] Ravi: Quantization primarily reduces model weights memory; KV entries are embeddings and attention caches which are affected by token size and data types. If you switch to lower precision for KV (float16 -> int8 packing) there are gains, but it's more complex and impacts numeric stability. We usually recommend model weight quantization first; KV quantization is experimental and we can discuss tradeoffs.

[06:10] Lena: For the paging thresholds, we recommend tuning max_kv_pages and enabling async prefetch for pages likely to be accessed soon (we can predict based on prefix patterns). That reduces latency spikes.

[06:30] Alex: Is async prefetch something you configure per-router or per-model?
[06:34] Ravi: Per-model routing policy; you can opt-in on heavy long-session models. There's a CPU/memory cost but it amortizes if you have predictable reuse.

[06:48] Priya: We're worried about worst-case tails — how do you handle graceful degradation?
[06:53] Maya: Our runtime has fallback policies: if a shard is overloaded we can route to a lower-cost model variant that has smaller KV footprint, or fall back to non-cached path. We also have rate-limit strategies per-tenant to protect shared nodes.

[07:10] Alex: Any quick config changes we can do now to test?
[07:13] Ravi: Three quick ones: 1) strip user-specific tokens from prefixes, 2) bump max_kv_pages for model shard by 25% in dedicated pool, 3) pin the most active sessions to a node subset for 24h and see eviction rate change.

[07:30] Tom: For privacy/compliance we need to keep things within our VPC. Does paging ever send KV to external storage?
[07:38] Ravi: No — in Private/VPC deployments paging stays on customer-controlled storage. In hosted we page to our encrypted SSDs; we can enable customer-managed KMS in Private mode for extra control.

[07:52] Priya: What logs should we share for you to reproduce the pattern?
[07:56] Ravi: We primarily need per-shard metrics (hit_ratio, eviction_rate, max_kv_pages, current_pages), timeline of token volume per session, and a few raw session traces. The logs we ask for are included in the runbook we'll share.

[08:12] Alex: Ok we'll extract those. Two more deep questions: 1) prefix reuse across restarts — is the cache persisted? 2) how do you handle long key lifetimes?
[08:23] Ravi: 1) Persistence: we persist cold pages to disk for dedicated/private nodes; after restarts the runtime reloads cold pages lazily. That means initial traffic after a restart may pay cold fetches but we avoid full warmup. 2) For lifetime we have TTL per-namespace; you can configure to keep keys longer if you expect reuse over days. Beware memory/paging tradeoff.

[08:50] Maya: Quick real-world anecdote: a customer had 10x unique prefixes because they logged request ids into prompt; after removing that they saw KV hit ratio jump from 28% to 76% and tail latency improved substantially.

[09:05] Priya: That's compelling. For our tests we'll try prefix normalization then run the benchmark.

[09:12] Ravi: We'll also try simulated increases to shard count in our sim harness. If you want we can run both options with your traces and show delta.

[09:22] Alex: Sounds good. On the topic of batching — does batching interact with KV cache warmed state?
[09:27] Ravi: Batching reduces per-token overhead but can increase memory pressure since a batch may touch multiple different prefixes simultaneously, causing more unique cache lookups. It's another tradeoff: larger batches = better throughput but potentially more cache churn.

[09:45] Priya: Any recommended batch sizes for long sessions?

[09:48] Ravi: For long-context interactive sessions we recommend moderate batch sizes (4-8) to avoid amplifying churn. Throughput-oriented backfills can use larger batches. We'll include batch guidance in the doc.

[10:05] Alex: One odd log we saw references 'prefix reuse collisions' — could that be misreporting?
[10:11] Ravi: Possibly; sometimes the monitoring aggregates per-shard and labels it 'prefix collision' when actually it's high cardinality. We'll validate metrics mapping in your exported logs.

[10:25] Tom: Any network considerations for storing cold pages? We use NFS on prem. Is that ok?
[10:30] Ravi: It works but we recommend local NVMe for faster rehydrate. If on NFS ensure low latency and bandwidth; remote paging will hurt tail latency.

[10:42] Maya: Okay let's recap next steps — Ravi will run a sim, Maya to share config & runbook, Zenon to export traces and per-shard logs, and we'll reconvene after the benchmark.

[10:55] Alex: One small Q: is there any automatic prefix normalization feature in Redwood or is that on the customer to implement?
[11:02] Ravi: We have helpers in the SDK for common normalizations (strip-tokens, canonicalize-whitespace, template placeholders) but full normalization is typically client-specific. We can offer a snippet you can drop in.

[11:15] Priya: Great. We'll try the SDK snippet. Thanks all.

[11:22] Maya: Thanks everyone. We'll send the runbook and schedule the follow-up.

End of transcript.
